strengths: The paper addresses an important phenomenon: good clean generalization can coexist with excellent adversarial training accuracy and poor adversarial test accuracy. The CGRO formulation makes this distinction explicit.

Partial signal learning combined with sample-specific noise memorization offers an interpretable hypothesis for this behavior. The proposed feature decomposition gives concrete quantities through which to investigate the hypothesis.

The experiments include model-size sweeps on MNIST and CIFAR10, synthetic feature-learning trajectories, and input-loss landscape diagnostics. These provide useful exploratory observations and illustrate the target generalization gap.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.4 is false under its stated assumptions. They permit a distribution supported on two separated points with an accurate but vulnerable linear clean classifier. With sufficiently many samples, both points have empirical frequencies near their population frequencies, so vanishing robust training error forces vanishing robust test error, contradicting CGRO. The proof lacks a condition ensuring that memorization leaves substantial population vulnerability. Moreover, Assumption 4.2 separates opposite classes only; it does not imply the claimed disjointness of all training neighborhoods. Appendix F also claims uniform vanishing-error approximation of a potentially discontinuous indicator-based classifier by continuous ReLU networks, which is generally impossible.

Theorem 5.9 does not establish robustness under the paper's definition. Definitions 5.4–5.6 restrict training attacks to the signal direction in the meaningful patch, whereas Definition 3.3 measures error over the entire perturbation ball. Appendix E.12 incorrectly infers small full-ball robust training error from small restricted adversarial loss. This distinction directly affects the proposed mechanism: under the stated signal-to-noise scaling, an ℓ2 attack can reverse the noise patches while shrinking the signal within the allowed radius, defeating a classifier whose adversarial training predictions rely on positive memorized noise margins.

The clean-generalization proof has additional substantive gaps. Appendix E.12 treats cubic forms of Gaussian variables as sub-Gaussian and applies an unjustified concentration bound; these forms generally have heavier tails, and different filters share the same noise. It also infers individual weight-norm bounds from aggregate memorization quantities without justification. Lemma E.11 absorbs σp²d into a polylogarithmic bound even though Assumption 5.7 permits cp < 1/2. Thus, restricting the robustness claim alone would not repair the dynamics theorem.

The claimed extension of the exponential lower bound beyond Li et al. (2022) is not demonstrated convincingly. Theorem 4.7 is existential, and Appendix F still constructs linearly separable data. An existing existential lower bound for that subclass already implies one for the broader class admitting polynomial-size clean classifiers. Furthermore, this worst-case construction is not connected to the structured distribution analyzed in Section 5 or to the empirical datasets, limiting the proposed explanation through representation complexity.

The experiments do not resolve these theoretical concerns. Section 6.2 uses δ = α = 10 despite the theorem requiring δ < α. This permits complete removal of the label-bearing signal, making poor robust population performance unavoidable and confounding the intended explanation through learning dynamics. The real-data capacity and flatness observations do not uniquely identify noise memorization as the cause. Reproduction and robustness assessment are also limited by missing PGD step counts, step sizes, restarts, repeated-run uncertainty, and complete training settings. These concerns affect the principal conclusions and prevent acceptance in the present form.
